title: Continuity at a Point (Formal Definition)
notes: **Formal statement.** f is continuous at x = a when lim(x→a) f(x) = f(a), which unpacks to LHL = RHL = f(a) with all three values finite.
**Epsilon form.** Equivalently, for every ε > 0 there exists δ > 0 such that |x − a| < δ implies |f(x) − f(a)| < ε; this is the definition used in proofs.
**Worked example.** For f(x) = kx + 1 when x ≤ 2 and f(x) = 3x − 1 when x > 2, set 2k + 1 = 5 to get k = 2 for continuity at 2.
**Checking boundaries.** Evaluate f(a) from the branch whose inequality includes equality, then compute the LHL and RHL from their respective branches.
**Consequences.** Continuity on a closed interval guarantees the function attains a maximum and a minimum (extreme value theorem) and takes every intermediate value.
**Exam caution.** A function can have a limit at a and still be discontinuous there; the missing condition is the equality lim = f(a).
summary: Formal continuity at a requires lim(x→a⁻) f = lim(x→a⁺) f = f(a); for piecewise rules this becomes an equation for the unknown parameter.
